sources.content: Asana has been an indoor climbing spot for the Treasure Valley at 4977 N. Glenwood St. since 2017. In June, the gym’s owner, Jamey Sproull, sent out the dreaded message to its climbers notifying them of the pending closure in November of this year. According to the message, Asana had “not been offered a new long-term lease agreement.” On Friday, Sproull sent out the good news in a message “I never thought I would be able to write.” According to the message, the property manager expressed a commitment to keeping Asana open at the current location. But there still are kinks to work out, Sproull said. A long-term lease agreement is not finalized yet, but Sproull stated that they have “every reason to believe” Asana will continue to operate at the location. [...] “When I announced that the gym would be closing, I did so because that was the reality we were facing,” Sproull stated in the message. “We had no long-term lease, no viable path to remain in the building, and no realistic alternative location that could support a climbing gym. It was one of the hardest announcements I have ever had to make.” Sproull said Asana will continue its regular operations and invest in the gym’s programs, youth climbing, competitions and events. He noted that the gym still has work to do as the agreement is finalized and will share updates. The “strength” of the climbing community helped Asana push through the weeks following the closure announcement, Sproull stated in the message. He thanked the gym’s members, staff, volunteers and the property manager. [...] The property is owned by TPC Glenwood, LLC, an affiliate of a developer and property manager that oversees businesses and housing in the Treasure Valley and across the western U.S. According to the closure message, the gym’s lease was originally set to expire at the end of June, but the property managers granted Asana an extension on the lease through the end of the year. sources.title: Garden City bouldering gym to close after lease dispute | Idaho Statesman
sources.content: A Boise-area rock climbing gym will close its doors later this year after more than a decade, citing leasing disagreements with the property manager and difficulty finding a new space. Asana Climbing Gym, which has operated at 4977 N Glenwood St. in Garden City since 2017, announced the closure to members of its mailing list via email on Tuesday. Owner Jamey Sproull wrote in the message that Asana has “not been offered a new long-term lease agreement” and will close on Nov. 29. Sproull did not immediately respond to a request for comment through the gym. [...] “As the owner of Asana Climbing Gym, I am deeply disappointed. Furthermore, as a climber, I am heartbroken,” Sproull said. He clarified that Asana Climbing — a separate business he operates that makes bouldering equipment — will stay in business. Asana shared an FAQ document online to address questions about memberships, future operations and other concerns, as well as a timeline for anticipated changes. According to the climbing gym’s website, Asana began as a manufacturing company in 1999 and in 2013 purchased The Front, a bouldering gym on Chinden Boulevard and 33rd Street in Garden City. It moved to its current location a few years later. [...] The property is owned by TPC Glenwood, LLC, which is affiliated with The Pacific Cos., a developer and property manager that oversees businesses and housing across the Treasure Valley and the West. The company did not respond to a request for comment on the leasing agreement with Asana or its future plans for the building. Sproull said he also looked for a new location for the gym during the lease process and came up empty-handed due to the niche zoning and height requirements needed to house the climbing gym or the “significantly higher lease rates” at plausible locations. He noted that Asana is financially stable and growing and said the closure is “not the result of any single event, disagreement, or the financial health or performance of the gym.”

(Reference Xu, Sherwin, Hall and Wu2016) further investigated the behaviour of incoming TS waves interacting with rapid localised base-flow distortions ( $\lt \mathcal{O}(\lambda \_x)$ , i.e. smaller than the streamwise wavelength of the perturbation). Here, the earlier hypothesised linear dependence of amplification on the surface feature height could not be reconciled by small humps and indentations both destabilising incoming TS waves. They observed a consistent stabilisation of the fundamental mode of cross-flow instability, defined as the most unstable mode in the baseline case (i.e. no hump present). Higher harmonics were instead consistently destabilised by the hump. Both behaviours were found to be governed by linear production mechanisms.
